action_criteria.expected_evidence: FVC 1.2 L (38% predicted; 16.6 mL/kg), MIP -18 cmH2O, MEP 28 cmH2O, weak cough
action_criteria.label: Measure respiratory function at the bedside now
action_criteria.rationale: Rapid bulbar and generalised weakness with dyspnoea: FVC, MIP and MEP decide ICU admission and elective intubation (20/30/40 rule, Lawn 2001).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Fluoroquinolone boxed warning for myasthenia gravis; stop ciprofloxacin; nitrofurantoin or fosfomycin as alternatives
action_criteria.label: Check ciprofloxacin as the precipitant
action_criteria.rationale: The deterioration began the day after ciprofloxacin was started; fluoroquinolones carry a boxed warning for myasthenia gravis, and the check also guides an MG-safe antibiotic.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Mild leukocytosis and CRP 14 mg/L; potassium, magnesium and phosphate normal; hypercapnic acidosis on ABG
action_criteria.label: Order blood count, electrolytes with magnesium and phosphate, CRP and a blood gas
action_criteria.rationale: Looks for infection and electrolyte disturbances that worsen neuromuscular transmission; the ABG shows hypercapnia, a late marker.

action_criteria.label: Repeat urine culture for persisting infection
action_criteria.rationale: Infection is the commonest crisis trigger; a persisting UTI would need an MG-safe antibiotic.

action_criteria.rationale: The diagnosis is established; a repeat titre does not change crisis management.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not continue ciprofloxacin or switch to another fluoroquinolone, an aminoglycoside or a macrolide for the urinary infection.

Avoid aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, macrolides and IV magnesium unless no alternative exists and the patient is monitored; use non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers only at reduced dose with quantitative monitoring.
Do not wait for oxygen saturation to fall or pCO2 to rise further before intubating when FVC, MIP and MEP are below the 20/30/40 thresholds.
Do not increase pyridostigmine to treat the crisis: it adds secretions and risks cholinergic weakness without treating the cause.
Do not start high-dose corticosteroids without ventilatory monitoring; they can worsen weakness in the first 1-2 weeks.
required_recommendations: Admit to the ICU and intubate electively now: FVC 16.6 mL/kg, MIP -18 cmH2O and MEP 28 cmH2O cross the 20/30/40 thresholds, with a weak cough and hypercapnia; if a neuromuscular blocker is needed, use a reduced dose of a non-depolarising agent with quantitative monitoring.
Stop ciprofloxacin and, if the urinary infection still needs treatment, complete it with an MG-safe antibiotic such as nitrofurantoin or fosfomycin.
Start plasma exchange (5 exchanges) or IVIG 2 g/kg over 2-5 days without delay.
Hold pyridostigmine while she is intubated to limit secretions and restart it at the previous dose when weaning.
Start corticosteroids under ventilatory monitoring, add a steroid-sparing agent (azathioprine after TPMT testing), and discuss thymectomy after recovery (AChR-positive generalised MG at 55, MGTX).
Give her a written list of drugs that worsen myasthenia gravis and ask her to tell every prescriber she has the condition.

key_clinical_evidence: Known AChR-positive generalised myasthenia gravis in remission on pyridostigmine alone, with ptosis, bulbar and limb weakness and dyspnoea starting the day after ciprofloxacin.
Bedside FVC 1.2 L (16.6 mL/kg), MIP -18 cmH2O and MEP 28 cmH2O with a weak cough: below the 20/30/40 thresholds.
ABG shows hypercapnic acidosis (pH 7.34, pCO2 52 mmHg), a late marker of ventilatory failure.
Fluoroquinolones carry an FDA boxed warning for exacerbation of myasthenia gravis.

alternatives: For E. coli cystitis susceptible to nitrofurantoin: nitrofurantoin or fosfomycin have no known effect on neuromuscular transmission.
interactions: Ciprofloxacin and myasthenia gravis: FDA boxed warning; fluoroquinolones may exacerbate muscle weakness in myasthenia gravis, and serious events including ventilatory failure have been reported, often within days of starting. Avoid in a patient with known myasthenia gravis; stop it.
Ciprofloxacin and levothyroxine: reduced levothyroxine absorption has been reported; minor.

patient.history_present_illness: A 55-year-old woman with AChR antibody-positive generalised myasthenia gravis, diagnosed 2 years ago, presented to the emergency department with acute respiratory distress and rapidly progressive generalized weakness. She had been doing well on pyridostigmine 60 mg three times daily alone, with minimal symptoms, for 18 months. Four days ago, she visited an urgent care clinic for dysuria and was diagnosed with a urinary tract infection. The urgent care provider sent a urine culture and prescribed ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily, which she started that evening; the culture grew E. coli susceptible to nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and ciprofloxacin, and her dysuria settled by day 2. The following morning, she noticed her ptosis was slightly worse. By day 2 of ciprofloxacin, her ptosis was severe and she could barely see. By day 3, she was unable to lift her arms above shoulder height and had severe difficulty swallowing. On the morning of presentation (day 4), her husband found her unable to get out of bed, gasping for breath, with oxygen saturation of 86% at home on pulse oximeter. She denied any recent fever (only the UTI), no new medications other than ciprofloxacin, no alcohol, no change in pyridostigmine dosing. She had not informed the urgent care provider of her MG diagnosis.
